content: Currently, palliative care models are being implemented in low-resource countries where the demand for care is high, but the availability of trained healthcare professionals, such as nurses and doctors, is limited. A common approach in these settings is to deliver care through community caregivers or volunteers who are supervised by nurses trained in palliative care. For example, the Neighborhood Network in Palliative Care in Kerala, India, and the Hospice and Palliative Care Association of South Africa have developed community-based, home-based care systems following this model. Ideally, any home care model should maintain strong connections to inpatient facilities for patients requiring more intensive symptom management or end-of-life care. For a palliative care program to succeed, education and training must align with the program's objectives and priorities. Since the complexity and scope of care vary across service levels, training must be tailored accordingly. For instance, if a program emphasizes home-based care, educational efforts should focus on raising community awareness and training healthcare workers, community leaders, and family caregivers in basic home care. Community-level healthcare workers should receive training and supervision from district-level professionals. Education should also coincide with the introduction of new services, such as making oral morphine and other essential medications available. Healthcare workers trained in palliative care often face challenges due to a lack of resources. To address this, in-service training can be organized in the target area with support from local authorities. This approach allows healthcare providers to remain connected to their work environment while contributing to the organization and implementation of palliative care services. When initiating a palliative care program in lowor middle-income countries, training should be provided to all healthcare workers in the target area. Palliative care requires expertise in communication, decision-making, managing treatment complications, pain and symptom management, psychosocial care, spiritual support, end-of-life care, and bereavement care. Numerous educational modules have been developed for healthcare professionals involved in palliative care, including community health workers, volunteers, nurses, physicians, medical students, pharmacists, health managers, and policymakers. Empowering family members and volunteers to act as palliative caregivers is a practical approach to achieving meaningful coverage, especially in rural areas. Family members and volunteers can also advocate for palliative care needs to local and national organizations. Training for families and volunteers should focus on personal care, social companionship, and applied medical care. For example, the Neighborhood Network in Palliative Care (NNPC) in Kerala, India, trains volunteers who dedicate at least two hours per week to care for the sick in their community. After completing structured training, volunteers form groups to identify and address the needs of chronically ill patients in their area. These groups are supported by trained doctors and nurses and work closely with existing palliative care facilities or establish new ones if necessary. Patients have the right to understand their end-of-life care options, including pain management and symptom control, to improve their quality of life. They should be informed that suffering is not inevitable and that appropriate treatment can significantly enhance their well-being. Public education is also essential to increase awareness of palliative care services and their benefits. Policymakers must recognize that palliative care is an integral part of the continuum of care for cancer and other diseases, can be integrated into existing healthcare systems at a relatively low cost, and requires the availability of opioids at all levels of care. Ensuring the availability of essential drugs for pain and symptom management is a critical component of a national palliative care plan. Policies should include a comprehensive list of essential medications to address common symptoms such as pain, nausea, vomiting, delirium, agitation, insomnia, fatigue, depression, and anxiety. These drugs should be included in the national essential medicines list, and their selection should be guided by a multidisciplinary team. Fear of opioid misuse often hinders their medical use, but clear policies and guidelines can help address this issue. Examples of successful palliative care initiatives include Uganda, which prioritized palliative care in its National Health Plan and made oral morphine widely available, even allowing nurses to prescribe it in rural areas. In India, Kerala has simplified licensing processes to improve morphine availability and established an integrated palliative care network. Romania has reformed its drug control policies to improve access to opioids for pain relief, balancing security with the need for modern medical practices. Standards should be evidence-based, measurable, and regularly monitored. They provide a common understanding of service quality, guide continuous improvement, and inform patients and families about the care they can expect. This requires careful planning, data collection, and the use of quality improvement frameworks. Evaluation plans should define who will evaluate the program, what will be evaluated, and how results will be used to improve performance. In conclusion, palliative care is a vital component of cancer control and should be integrated into prevention, early detection, and treatment strategies. Evidence-based standards and low-cost public health models can extend palliative care to underserved populations, particularly in low-resource settings. WHO encourages countries to share their successes and seek guidance to address their specific needs.
